title: Statistics: Seeing Beyond the Peaks and Valleys
text:
A dataset can be imagined as a mountain range filled with peaks and valleys.
Each value rises and falls across the landscape. From a close view, it appears irregular and scattered, but from a higher perspective, its true structure becomes clear. Statistics helps us step back and reveal the hidden patterns within variation.

title: Interactive Demographic and Health Data Dashboard for Australia
text:
Demographic and health data play a vital role in understanding population dynamics, monitoring public health, and supporting evidence-based decision-making worldwide. By transforming complex, publicly available datasets into an accessible and interactive platform, this dashboard enables users to explore demographic patterns, health outcomes, and population dynamics with ease. It was developed under the guidance of Dr. Chathuri Jayasinghe as part of the STA 322 2.0 Medical Statistics (2025/26) course.
The dashboard is designed to support students, researchers, policymakers, and the general public in understanding Australia’s demographic transition and the changing health profile of its population. Through interactive visualizations, it demonstrates the country’s progression through different stages of demographic transition while highlighting emerging challenges and opportunities related to population ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration.
These demographic trends have important implications for economic growth, labour force dynamics, pension sustainability, healthcare systems, and the demand for social services. By presenting data in a clear and engaging format, the dashboard facilitates evidence-based decision-making, promotes a better understanding of public health and demographic issues, and serves as a valuable resource for academic learning, research, and policy planning.

title: Creating a User-Defined Python Module: Reusing Code the Right Way
text:
As your Python programs become larger, you will often find yourself writing the same functions repeatedly. For example, you might create functions to perform calculations, process data, or convert units. Copying these functions into every new script is not a good practice because it makes your code harder to maintain.
A better approach is to place reusable code in a module. A user-defined module is simply a Python file (.py) that contains functions, variables, or classes created by the user. Once the module is created, it can be imported into other Python scripts, allowing you to reuse the same code without rewriting it.
In this post, we’ll create our own module and learn how to use it in another Python script.

title: Creating a User-Defined Python Module: Reusing Code the Right Way
Creating a User-Defined Python Module: Reusing Code the Right Way
text:
Step 2: Use the Module
Now create another Python file in the same folder and import the module.

import calc 

print(calc.add(10, 2)) 
print(calc.subtract(10, 2))

12
8


Notice that each function is accessed using the module name followed by a dot (.). This tells Python that the functions add() and subtract() are defined inside the calc module.

title: Creating a User-Defined Python Module: Reusing Code the Right Way
text:
Importing Specific Functions
Sometimes you only need one or two functions from a module. Instead of importing the entire module, you can import only the functions you need.

from calc import add 

print(add(5, 3))

8


You can also import multiple functions at once.

from calc import add, subtract 

print(add(7, 4)) 
print(subtract(7, 4))

11
3


Since the functions are imported directly, there is no need to use the calc. prefix.

title: Creating a User-Defined Python Module: Reusing Code the Right Way
text:
Why Use User-Defined Modules?
Using your own modules has several advantages:

Avoid writing the same code multiple times.
Keep related functions together in one file.
Make programs easier to read and organize.
Reuse functions in multiple Python scripts stored in the same project.


Final Thoughts
A user-defined module is simply a Python file that contains reusable code. Instead of copying the same functions into every script, you can write them once, save them in a module, and import them whenever they are needed. This approach helps you write cleaner, more organized, and easier-to-maintain programs.
Although this example contains only two simple functions, the same idea applies to much larger programs. Organizing your code into modules is a fundamental programming practice that will become increasingly valuable as your projects grow in size and complexity.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text: In this blog post, we explore the complete workflow of building a structured website using Quarto, based on a real project: the R Learning Website.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Overview of the Workflow

Building a Quarto website involves four main steps:

Creating a Quarto project
Structuring content into .qmd files
Configuring the website using _quarto.yml
Rendering and publishing the website

We will explain each step using the R Learning Website as an example.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
section: Step 1: Creating the Quarto Website Project
text:
Step 1: Creating the Quarto Website Project

The project is initialized using RStudio:
File → New Project → New Directory → Quarto Website
This automatically generates the basic structure:
R-Learning-Website/
│── index.qmd
│── about.qmd
│── _quarto.yml
│── styles.css
In your case, additional learning modules can be added as individual .qmd files:
Introduction to R and RStudio.qmd
Data Types and Data Structures.qmd 
Data Import and Export.qmd
Reshaping Data with tidyr.qmd
Data Manipulation with dplyr.qmd
Data Visualization with ggplot2.qmd
Statistical Modeling in R.qmd
Reproduciable Reporting with Quarto.qmd
...

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Step 2: Adding Content Pages

The homepage (index.qmd) introduces the website:
---
title: "R Learning Website"
---

## Welcome 👋

This website is a structured learning resource for **R programming and statistics**.

It includes step-by-step modules covering: - Data manipulation - Visualization - Statistical modeling - Reproducible reporting using Quarto

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

This website is **an illustrative example** used to demonstrate the process of building a Quarto website. It is intended for learning purposes only. You can customize its structure, content, layout, and design to suit your own project or personal website.
:::
The about.qmd file typically contains author or project details.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Step 3: Organizing Content into Modules

Each .qmd file represents a learning unit in your website.
For example, a module like Introduction to R and RStudio.qmd contains:
---
title: "Introduction to R and RStudio"
---

## Introduction

R is a powerful programming language designed for statistical computing, data analysis, and data visualization. RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) that provides a user-friendly interface for writing, running, and managing R code.

## Topics Covered

- What is R?
- What is RStudio?
- Installing R and RStudio
- Understanding the RStudio interface
- Running your first R commands

## Example

```r
# Assign values to variables
x <- 10
y <- 20

# Perform a simple calculation
sum <- x + y

# Display the result
print(sum)
```

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Step 4: Configuring the Website (_quarto.yml)

The _quarto.yml file controls navigation and layout.
In your R Learning Website, the structure is defined like this:

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs

website:
  title: "R Learning Website"

  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home

      - href: about.qmd
        text: About

      - text: Learning Modules
        menu:
          - href: "Intrduction to R and RStudio.qmd"
            text: Introduction to R and RStudio

          - href: "Data Types and Data Structures.qmd"
            text: Data Types and Data Structures

          - href: "Data Import and Export.qmd"
            text: Data Import and Export

          - href: "Reshaping Data with tidyr.qmd"
            text: Reshaping Data with tidyr

          - href: "Data Manipulation with dplyr.qmd"
            text: Data Manipulation with dplyr

          - href: "Data Visualization with ggplot2.qmd"
            text: Data Visualization with ggplot2

          - href: "Statistical Modeling in R.qmd"
            text: Statistical Modeling in R

          - href: "Reproducible Reporting with Quarto.qmd"
            text: Reproducible Reporting with Quarto

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
    toc: true
    
Here,

project: defines the project type and specifies that the rendered website should be placed in the docs directory.



website: contains the website title and navigation bar.



navbar: creates the menu that links to each learning module.



format: controls the appearance of the website, including the theme, custom CSS, and table of contents.

In this example, the website output is directed to the docs folder using output-dir: docs. This is recommended because it simplifies deployment with GitHub Pages, allowing the rendered website to be published directly from the docs directory.
Important: YAML is indentation-sensitive, meaning that the hierarchy of the configuration is determined by spaces rather than braces or parentheses. Therefore, it is essential to maintain consistent indentation throughout the _ quarto.yml file. Incorrect indentation may result in configuration errors or prevent the website from rendering successfully.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Step 5: Previewing the Website

While developing, you can preview the website using:
quarto preview
This opens a live local server where changes are updated automatically.

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
text:
Step 6: Rendering the Website

To generate the final static website:
quarto render
This creates the output in the docs/ folder:
docs/
│── index.html
│── about.html
│── Introduction to R and RStudio.html
│── ...

title: Building Your First Website with Quarto: A Step-by-Step Guide
section: Step 7: Publishing the Website with GitHub Pages
text:
Step 7: Publishing the Website with GitHub Pages

Quarto provides several options for publishing websites, including Posit Connect Cloud, GitHub Pages, Posit Connect, Quarto Pub, and Netlify. In this post, we will use GitHub Pages because it is free, beginner-friendly, and integrates seamlessly with GitHub repositories.

Prerequisite
Before publishing your website, make sure your Quarto project is stored in a GitHub repository. This allows GitHub Pages to access your project and publish your website.
A typical workflow is:
Create Quarto Website
        ↓
Initialize Git Repository
        ↓
Push Project to GitHub
        ↓
Render Website
        ↓
Enable GitHub Pages
Once your project is available on GitHub, you are ready to publish the website.


Enable GitHub Pages
Quarto provides both terminal-based commands and the GitHub web interface for deploying websites. While the terminal approach is useful for experienced users and automated workflows, the GitHub web interface is more intuitive for beginners. Therefore, in this post, we will use the GitHub interface to deploy the website.
Open your GitHub repository and follow these steps:

Navigate to Settings.





Select Pages from the left sidebar.





Under Build and deployment, choose:

Source: Deploy from a branch

Then select:

Branch: master
Folder: /docs

Click Save.






GitHub will automatically begin publishing your website. After a few moments, the website URL will appear at the top of the Pages settings page.





Note: We select the /docs folder because our Quarto project is configured with output-dir: docs in _quarto.yml. This ensures that GitHub Pages publishes the rendered HTML files generated by Quarto.

title: Forecasting Commodity Net Export Price Index (CNEPI)
text: This project focuses on forecasting the Commodity Net Export Price Index (CNEPI) for Sri Lanka using ARIMA time series models. The CNEPI is constructed by weighting individual commodity prices by their net export share relative to GDP.

title: Forecasting Commodity Net Export Price Index (CNEPI)
text:
Objectives

The main objective of this project is to build a simple and easily interpretable model so that the business community can use it to make effective decisions.
This project was conducted as part of the Research Methodology course unit. Hence we applied research methodology principles rigorously throughout the project. Since this was done at the beginning of our third year, we initially had no theoretical knowledge of ARIMA models, but through extensive self-study, we learned the correct methodology for ARIMA modeling. This process significantly improved our literature review, report writing, and research skills.

title: Forecasting Commodity Net Export Price Index (CNEPI)
text:
Methodology


Preliminary (Exploratory) Analysis
Test for Stationarity
Choosing and Fitting Models
Model Evaluation
Residual Diagnostics
Forecasting Future Values

Throughout this project, we followed the methodology outlined in Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.) by Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021). Figure 1 illustrates the exact forecasting workflow adopted in this study.




Figure 1: General process for forecasting using an ARIMA model (Adapted from Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021)

title: Forecasting Commodity Net Export Price Index (CNEPI)
text:
Results


The ARIMA(2,1,3) model was identified as the most suitable forecasting model based on the model selection criteria. The fitted model is given by:


\[
Y_t = -0.0022 + BY_t + 0.1130(1-B)BY_t + 0.8485(1-B)B^2Y_t + 0.1279BZ_t - 0.9217B^2Z_t - 0.2062B^3Z_t + Z_t
\]


Residual tests proved the model works correctly.
The forecasts suggest a gradual upward trend, with values rising from 100.81 in April 2025 to 100.92 by March 2026. This indicates a modest recovery and stabilization of Sri Lanka’s net export competitiveness





Figure 2: Fitting and Prediction of the Commodity Net Export Price Index

title: DS Job Tracker Survey
text:
The DS Job Tracker Survey was conducted to collect, organize, and analyze job advertisements related to data science and statistics. By systematically extracting information from job postings and transforming it into a structured, study-ready dataset, the project provides valuable insights into the qualifications, technical skills, programming languages, software tools, and experience commonly requested by employers. It serves as a practical resource for students, graduates, and professionals seeking to understand current industry expectations and identify the competencies most sought after in the data science job market.
Throughout this project, I strengthened my skills in data collection, data wrangling, and data preprocessing while working with real-world job advertisement data. The project also provided an opportunity to explore trends in job postings, compare skill requirements across different roles, and gain a better understanding of the knowledge and technical expertise required to pursue a career in data science and statistics.

title: DS Job Tracker Survey
section: Job Ad Data Collector (R Shiny App)
text:
Job Ad Data Collector (R Shiny App)

Job advertisement data for this project were collected collaboratively by a group of twelve students, including myself. As part of the project, I designed and developed an R Shiny application to support the data collection process. The application provides a simple and structured interface for recording information from data science and analytics job advertisements, ensuring consistency in the collected data. All entries are automatically stored in a connected Google Sheet, enabling efficient and centralized data management.
Job Ad Data Collector

title: DS Job Tracker Survey
text:
Collected Datasets

The project involved ten groups, with each group independently collecting data related to data science and analytics job advertisements. After data collection, we (Group_1) performed data preprocessing, cleaning, and standardization, and then combined all group datasets into a single unified dataset for analysis. This final dataset provides a comprehensive and structured view of the collected job advertisement information. All individual group datasets, along with the final cleaned dataset prepared by our group, are available for reference.
